Radar Cross Section (RCS) is critical for military stealth and radar detection as well as civilian RFID and antenna characterization.
Reverberation Chambers (RCs) provide a diffuse electromagnetic field environment for RCS measurements.
The method uses the difference between reflection coefficients measured with and without the target at the same stirrer position.
The stirrer inside the RC creates a varying multipath environment affecting the backscattered signals.
Measurements were conducted in the 9.75 GHz to 10.25 GHz frequency range.
The target was a metallic plate placed 2.95 meters from the horn antenna.
The horn antenna was vertically polarized and oriented toward the target.
The RCS pattern obtained in the RC matched well with the Anechoic Chamber results, except at very low RCS levels.
The transfer function H(f, θ_st) follows a normal Gaussian distribution with respect to frequency.
The ballistic wave amplitude is modeled using Friis equation considering antenna gain, wavelength, and distance.
Stirrer position shifts greater than 20° cause significant errors in RCS estimation.
For stirrer position shifts above 32.4°, RCS pattern extraction becomes impossible.
The method avoids time gating and Fourier transform by working directly in the frequency domain.
The difference signal shows an oscillatory pattern corresponding to the ballistic wave.
The study recommends using the same stirrer position for measurements with and without the target to ensure accuracy.
The RC method is a cost-effective alternative to Anechoic Chambers for canonical target RCS measurement.
The antenna reflection coefficient S(f, θ_st) includes free-space reflection and backscattering from the chamber.
The phase term in the ballistic wave accounts for the two-way travel distance between antenna and target.
The method assumes the target size is much smaller than the antenna-target distance.
